items.stem: What is meant by “breathing”?
items.answer: The process of exchange of O₂ from the atmosphere with CO₂ produced by the cells.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the process of exchange of O₂ from the atmosphere with CO₂ produced by the cells.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about respiratory organs and the human respiratory system is correct?
items.answer: Earthworms use their moist cuticle for gas exchange.
items.markingKey: (c) Earthworms use their moist cuticle for gas exchange. The other statements are false. It is supported by incomplete (C-shaped) cartilaginous rings. Gas exchange occurs in the alveoli; the trachea and bronchi only conduct air. Insects respire through a network of tracheal tubes.
options: The trachea is supported by complete cartilaginous rings.
Earthworms use their moist cuticle for gas exchange.
Gas exchange occurs in the trachea and bronchi.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT an animal that respires through gills?
items.answer: insects
items.markingKey: (b) Insects is an animal that respires through tracheal tubes, not an animal that respires through gills.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “The pleura increases friction on the lung surface.”
items.answer: Pleural fluid reduces friction on the lung surface.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: Pleural fluid reduces friction on the lung surface.

items.stem: Which of the following shows the correct path of air through the human respiratory system?
items.answer: pharynx → trachea → alveoli
items.markingKey: (d) pharynx → trachea → alveoli. Air passes from nostrils to the alveoli.

items.stem:
A part of the human respiratory system has these features: straight tube extending to the mid-thoracic cavity; supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings; part of the conducting zone.
(i) Identify the part. (1 mark)
(ii) State one more feature you would expect to observe. (1 mark)
(iii) How would the observations differ if it were the larynx? Give two points. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) The trachea (ii) divides at the fifth thoracic vertebra (iii) opening covered by the epiglottis during swallowing; also called the sound box
items.markingKey: (i) the trachea – 1 mark. (ii) any one of: divides at the fifth thoracic vertebra – 1 mark. (iii) for the larynx: cartilaginous box; helps in sound production; also called the sound box – 1 mark each for any two.

items.stem: Which of the following is an animal that respires through lungs?
items.answer: birds
items.markingKey: (c) Birds is an animal that respires through lungs; the others are not.

items.stem: A part of the human respiratory system has these features: outer layer in contact with the thoracic lining; double-layered covering of the lungs. Identify the part. Give a reason.
items.answer: The pleura
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the pleura; 1 mark: the features outer layer in contact with the thoracic lining; double-layered covering of the lungs are characteristic of it.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as animal that respires through gills or animal that respires through tracheal tubes: fishes, insects, many molluscs.
items.answer: fishes – animal that respires through gills; insects – animal that respires through tracheal tubes; many molluscs – animal that respires through gills.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: fishes – animal that respires through gills; insects – animal that respires through tracheal tubes; many molluscs – animal that respires through gills.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as animal that respires through the body surface or animal that respires through gills: coelenterates, flatworms, sponges, many molluscs.
items.answer: coelenterates – animal that respires through the body surface; flatworms – animal that respires through the body surface; sponges – animal that respires through the body surface; many molluscs – animal that respires through gills.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: coelenterates – animal that respires through the body surface; flatworms – animal that respires through the body surface; sponges – animal that respires through the body surface; many molluscs – animal that respires through gills.

items.stem: Which of the following is an animal that respires through the body surface?
items.answer: coelenterates
items.markingKey: (a) Coelenterates is an animal that respires through the body surface; the others are not.

items.stem: Define the term “alveoli”.
items.answer: Very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures at the ends of bronchioles where gases are exchanged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures at the ends of bronchioles where gases are exchanged.

items.stem: Define the term “inspiration”.
items.answer: The process by which atmospheric air is drawn into the lungs when intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the process by which atmospheric air is drawn into the lungs when intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as pulmonary capacity or respiratory volume: expiratory reserve volume, inspiratory reserve volume, tidal volume, total lung capacity.
items.answer: expiratory reserve volume – respiratory volume; inspiratory reserve volume – respiratory volume; tidal volume – respiratory volume; total lung capacity – pulmonary capacity.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: expiratory reserve volume – respiratory volume; inspiratory reserve volume – respiratory volume; tidal volume – respiratory volume; total lung capacity – pulmonary capacity.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Tidal volume is about 3000 mL.
Reason (R): Residual volume cannot be measured directly with a spirometer.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false: Tidal volume is about 500 mL; IRV is 2500–3000 mL. R is a true statement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “During inspiration the diaphragm relaxes.”
items.answer: The diaphragm contracts and flattens during inspiration; it relaxes during expiration.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: The diaphragm contracts and flattens during inspiration; it relaxes during expiration.

items.stem: Define (i) inspiratory capacity, (ii) functional residual capacity and (iii) total lung capacity, giving the formula for each.
items.answer: (i) IC = TV + IRV – total air a person can inspire after a normal expiration; (ii) FRC = ERV + RV – air remaining in the lungs after a normal expiration; (iii) TLC = RV + ERV + TV + IRV or VC + RV – total air accommodated in the lungs after a forced inspiration.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: A person breathes 16 times a minute with a tidal volume of 600 mL. How much air does the person inspire or expire per minute and per hour?
items.answer: 9600 mL per minute (9.6 L); 576 L per hour
items.markingKey: Volume per minute = TV × rate = 600 × 16 = 9600 mL (1); per hour = 9600 × 60 = 576000 mL = 576 L (1).

items.stem:
At a sports medicine clinic in Pune, a swimmer blew into a spirometer. After a normal breath out, she exhaled forcibly an extra 1200 mL; her normal breath was 550 mL and after a normal breath in she could inhale an additional 3300 mL.
(i) Name the three volumes measured. (1 mark)
(ii) Calculate her vital capacity. (2 marks)
(iii) Why can a spirometer not measure her total lung capacity directly? (1 mark)
items.answer: (i) ERV = 1200 mL, TV = 550 mL, IRV = 3300 mL. (ii) VC = ERV + TV + IRV = 1200 + 550 + 3300 = 5050 mL. (iii) TLC includes the residual volume, which always remains in the lungs and cannot be exhaled.

items.stem: For a healthy person, TV = 450 mL, IRV = 3000 mL, ERV = 1100 mL and RV = 1100 mL. What is the expiratory capacity (EC)?
items.markingKey: (c) expiratory capacity (EC) = TV + ERV = 1550 mL.

items.stem: Arrange the following in the correct sequence of events in inspiration: intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric, thoracic volume increases, diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract. Give a reason.
items.answer: diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract → thoracic volume increases → intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the order diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract → thoracic volume increases → intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric; 1 mark for the reason: Volume up, pressure down, air in.

items.stem: Which of the following is a respiratory volume?
items.answer: expiratory reserve volume
items.markingKey: (b) Expiratory reserve volume is a respiratory volume; the others are not.

items.stem: A person breathes 18 times a minute with a tidal volume of 550 mL. How much air does the person inspire or expire per minute and per hour?
items.answer: 9900 mL per minute (9.9 L); 594 L per hour
items.markingKey: Volume per minute = TV × rate = 550 × 18 = 9900 mL (1); per hour = 9900 × 60 = 594000 mL = 594 L (1).

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the mechanism of breathing and respiratory volumes is correct?
items.answer: Inspiration is initiated by the contraction of the diaphragm, which increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis.
items.markingKey: (a) Inspiration is initiated by the contraction of the diaphragm, which increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis. The other statements are false. Inspiration occurs when it is lower; expiration when it is higher. VC = ERV + TV + IRV; total lung capacity includes RV. Tidal volume is about 500 mL; IRV is 2500–3000 mL.
options: Inspiration is initiated by the contraction of the diaphragm, which increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis.
Vital capacity includes the residual volume.
Inspiration occurs when intra-pulmonary pressure is higher than atmospheric pressure.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between inspiration and expiration on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A phase of breathing has these features: diaphragm contracts and flattens. Identify the phase – inspiration or expiration? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) Inspiration: diaphragm contracts and flattens; external intercostal muscles contract; thoracic and pulmonary volumes increase. Expiration: diaphragm relaxes and returns to dome shape; intercostal muscles relax; thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease. (b) Inspiration.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: inspiration; 1 mark: “diaphragm contracts and flattens” is a feature of inspiration.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a pulmonary capacity?
items.answer: residual volume
items.markingKey: (d) Residual volume is a respiratory volume, not a pulmonary capacity.

items.stem: Give two differences between inspiration and expiration.
items.answer: Inspiration: external intercostal muscles contract; diaphragm contracts and flattens. Expiration: diaphragm relaxes and returns to dome shape; intra-pulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. inspiration – external intercostal muscles contract; diaphragm contracts and flattens; expiration – diaphragm relaxes and returns to dome shape; intra-pulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric.

items.stem: A phase of breathing has these features: diaphragm relaxes and returns to dome shape; intercostal muscles relax; thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease. Identify the phase. Give a reason.
items.answer: Expiration
items.markingKey: 1 mark: expiration; 1 mark: the features diaphragm relaxes and returns to dome shape; intercostal muscles relax; thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease are characteristic of it.

items.stem: What is meant by “respiratory rhythm centre”?
items.answer: A specialised centre in the medulla region of the brain primarily responsible for regulating breathing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a specialised centre in the medulla region of the brain primarily responsible for regulating breathing.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the exchange and transport of gases and the regulation of respiration is correct?
items.answer: The solubility of CO₂ is 20–25 times higher than that of O₂.
items.markingKey: (a) The solubility of CO₂ is 20–25 times higher than that of O₂. The other statements are false. Alveolar pO₂ (104 mm Hg) is higher than in deoxygenated blood (40 mm Hg), so O₂ diffuses into blood. About 70% of CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate; 20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin. Low pCO₂, high pO₂, lower H⁺ and lower temperature favour oxyhaemoglobin formation, as in the alveoli.
options: The solubility of CO₂ is 20–25 times higher than that of O₂.
High pCO₂ and high H⁺ favour the formation of oxyhaemoglobin.
Most CO₂ is carried as carbamino-haemoglobin.
pO₂ in the alveoli is lower than in the deoxygenated blood.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Oxygen plays an insignificant role in the regulation of respiratory rhythm.
Reason (R): Most CO₂ is carried as carbamino-haemoglobin.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is true, but R is false.
items.markingKey: (c) A is true. R is false: About 70% of CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate; 20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Conditions at a site in the body are: low pCO₂ (40 mm Hg); lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature; high pO₂ (104 mm Hg). Identify the site. Give a reason.
items.answer: The alveoli
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the alveoli; 1 mark: the features low pCO₂ (40 mm Hg); lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature; high pO₂ (104 mm Hg) are characteristic of it.

items.stem:

Reason (R): Increase in CO₂ and H⁺ activates the chemosensitive area.

items.markingKey: (d) It is sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺, not O₂; R is true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem:

(i) Identify the site. (1 mark)
(ii) State one more feature you would expect to observe. (1 mark)
(iii) How would the observations differ if it were the tissues? Give two points. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) The alveoli (ii) oxyhaemoglobin is formed (iii) low pO₂ (40 mm Hg); oxyhaemoglobin dissociates
items.markingKey: (i) the alveoli – 1 mark. (ii) any one of: oxyhaemoglobin is formed – 1 mark. (iii) for the tissues: low pO₂ (40 mm Hg); high pCO₂ (45 mm Hg); high H⁺ concentration and higher temperature – 1 mark each for any two.

items.stem: Explain the transport of O₂ and CO₂ in blood. Describe the factors affecting the binding of O₂ with haemoglobin.
items.answer: O₂: 97% as oxyhaemoglobin (each Hb binds up to four O₂), 3% dissolved in plasma; dissociation curve sigmoid; alveoli – high pO₂, low pCO₂, low H⁺, lower temperature → binding; tissues – opposite → dissociation; 5 mL O₂ per 100 mL blood. CO₂: 20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin, 70% as bicarbonate via carbonic anhydrase (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺), 7% dissolved; 4 mL CO₂ per 100 mL deoxygenated blood released at alveoli.
items.markingKey: 2 marks O₂; 2 marks CO₂; 1 mark factors.

items.stem: Which term describes the sigmoid curve obtained when percentage saturation of haemoglobin with O₂ is plotted against pO₂?
items.answer: oxygen dissociation curve
items.markingKey: (b) Oxygen dissociation curve: the sigmoid curve obtained when percentage saturation of haemoglobin with O₂ is plotted against pO₂.

items.stem: Explain the role of carbonic anhydrase in the transport of CO₂.
items.answer: Present in high concentration in RBCs (and in small amounts in plasma). At tissues, high pCO₂: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺; bicarbonate carried in plasma. At alveoli, low pCO₂: reaction reverses, releasing CO₂ and H₂O, and CO₂ is exhaled.
items.markingKey: 1 mark location; 1 mark tissues; 1 mark alveoli.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the exchange and transport of gases and the regulation of respiration is incorrect?

options: Every 100 mL of oxygenated blood can deliver around 5 mL of O₂ to the tissues under normal physiological conditions.
Oxygen plays an insignificant role in the regulation of respiratory rhythm.
The diffusion membrane is made of three major layers: alveolar squamous epithelium, endothelium of capillaries and the basement substance between them.

items.stem: Define the term “fibrosis”.
items.answer: Proliferation of fibrous tissue that causes serious lung damage after long exposure to dust.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about disorders of the respiratory system is correct?

items.stem:
Ramesh, who has worked for 20 years in a stone-crushing unit near Jodhpur without a mask, now has a persistent cough and breathlessness. His X-ray shows scarring of the lungs.
(i) Name the likely disorder. (1 mark)
(ii) What type of disorder is it? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how it damages the lungs and suggest two preventive measures. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Silicosis. (ii) Occupational respiratory disorder. (iii) Long exposure to silica dust causes inflammation leading to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissue), reducing lung function; wear protective masks, use dust control/wet methods, regular health check-ups.

items.stem: Give three differences between occupational respiratory disorders and asthma.
items.answer: Occupational respiratory disorders: prevented by protective masks; e.g. silicosis and asbestosis; caused by dust at the workplace. Asthma: may be triggered by allergens; wheezing; difficulty in breathing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each of three correct, paired points of difference, e.g. occupational respiratory disorders – prevented by protective masks; e.g. silicosis and asbestosis; caused by dust at the workplace; asthma – may be triggered by allergens; wheezing; difficulty in breathing.

items.stem: Describe asthma, emphysema and occupational respiratory disorders. Suggest measures to prevent them.
items.answer: Asthma – wheezing and breathing difficulty due to inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles; avoid allergens. Emphysema – chronic; alveolar walls damaged, respiratory surface decreased; smoking a major cause; avoid smoking. Occupational – silicosis, asbestosis from long exposure to dust in grinding or stone-breaking industries; inflammation, fibrosis; protective masks, dust control.

items.stem: A phase of breathing has these features: thoracic and pulmonary volumes increase; diaphragm contracts and flattens; intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric. Identify the phase. Give a reason.
items.answer: Inspiration
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inspiration; 1 mark: the features thoracic and pulmonary volumes increase; diaphragm contracts and flattens; intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric are characteristic of it.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between the tissues and the alveoli on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) Conditions at a site in the body are: high pCO₂ (45 mm Hg). Identify the site – the tissues or the alveoli? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) The tissues: low pO₂ (40 mm Hg); high pCO₂ (45 mm Hg); high H⁺ concentration and higher temperature. The alveoli: high pO₂ (104 mm Hg); low pCO₂ (40 mm Hg); lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature. (b) The tissues.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: the tissues; 1 mark: “high pCO₂ (45 mm Hg)” is a feature of the tissues.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about disorders of the respiratory system is incorrect?
items.answer: Asthma is caused by damage to alveolar walls.
items.markingKey: (a) The incorrect statement is “Asthma is caused by damage to alveolar walls.” Correct form: Asthma is due to inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles; emphysema damages alveolar walls.
options: Asthma is caused by damage to alveolar walls.
Asthma causes wheezing due to inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles.
Workers in stone-breaking or grinding industries should wear protective masks.
Long exposure to dust can give rise to inflammation leading to fibrosis.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as pulmonary capacity or respiratory volume: expiratory reserve volume, functional residual capacity, inspiratory reserve volume, tidal volume.
items.answer: expiratory reserve volume – respiratory volume; functional residual capacity – pulmonary capacity; inspiratory reserve volume – respiratory volume; tidal volume – respiratory volume.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: expiratory reserve volume – respiratory volume; functional residual capacity – pulmonary capacity; inspiratory reserve volume – respiratory volume; tidal volume – respiratory volume.

items.stem: A respiratory disorder shows these features: inflammation leading to fibrosis; caused by dust at the workplace; e.g. silicosis and asbestosis. Identify the disorder. Give a reason.
items.answer: Occupational respiratory disorders
items.markingKey: 1 mark: occupational respiratory disorders; 1 mark: the features inflammation leading to fibrosis; caused by dust at the workplace; e.g. silicosis and asbestosis are characteristic of it.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The trachea is supported by complete cartilaginous rings.
Reason (R): The thoracic chamber is anatomically an air-tight chamber.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false: It is supported by incomplete (C-shaped) cartilaginous rings. R is a true statement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Explain the term “carbonic anhydrase”.
items.answer: An enzyme in RBCs that catalyses the reversible formation of carbonic acid from CO₂ and water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: an enzyme in RBCs that catalyses the reversible formation of carbonic acid from CO₂ and water.

items.stem:
A phase of breathing has these features: external intercostal muscles contract; diaphragm contracts and flattens; intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric.
(i) Identify the phase. (1 mark)
(ii) State one more feature you would expect to observe. (1 mark)
(iii) How would the observations differ if it were expiration? Give two points. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Inspiration (ii) thoracic and pulmonary volumes increase (iii) intercostal muscles relax; thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease
items.markingKey: (i) inspiration – 1 mark. (ii) any one of: thoracic and pulmonary volumes increase – 1 mark. (iii) for expiration: diaphragm relaxes and returns to dome shape; intercostal muscles relax; thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease – 1 mark each for any two.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “The respiratory rhythm centre is in the pons.”
items.answer: It is in the medulla; the pneumotaxic centre is in the pons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: It is in the medulla; the pneumotaxic centre is in the pons.

items.stem: Which of the following is a pulmonary capacity?
items.answer: functional residual capacity
items.markingKey: (d) Functional residual capacity is a pulmonary capacity; the others are not.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “Dust in industries does not affect the respiratory system.”
items.answer: Long exposure to dust can cause inflammation and fibrosis of the lungs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: Long exposure to dust can cause inflammation and fibrosis of the lungs.

items.stem:
A respiratory disorder shows these features: difficulty in breathing; wheezing; inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles.
(i) Identify the disorder. (1 mark)
(ii) State one more feature you would expect to observe. (1 mark)
(iii) How would the observations differ if it were occupational respiratory disorders? Give two points. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Asthma (ii) may be triggered by allergens (iii) caused by dust at the workplace; prevented by protective masks
items.markingKey: (i) asthma – 1 mark. (ii) any one of: may be triggered by allergens – 1 mark. (iii) for occupational respiratory disorders: caused by dust at the workplace; e.g. silicosis and asbestosis; inflammation leading to fibrosis – 1 mark each for any two.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about respiratory organs and the human respiratory system is correct?
items.answer: Frogs can respire through their moist skin.
items.markingKey: (d) Frogs can respire through their moist skin. The other statements are false. It is supported by incomplete (C-shaped) cartilaginous rings. Gas exchange occurs in the alveoli; the trachea and bronchi only conduct air. Pleural fluid reduces friction on the lung surface.
options: Gas exchange occurs in the trachea and bronchi.
The trachea is supported by complete cartilaginous rings.
The pleura increases friction on the lung surface.
Frogs can respire through their moist skin.

items.stem: For a healthy person, TV = 450 mL, IRV = 3200 mL, ERV = 1100 mL and RV = 1300 mL. What is the vital capacity (VC)?
items.markingKey: (a) vital capacity (VC) = ERV + TV + IRV = 4750 mL.

items.stem: Explain the term “tidal volume”.
items.answer: The volume of air inspired or expired during a normal respiration, approximately 500 mL.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the volume of air inspired or expired during a normal respiration, approximately 500 mL.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between the trachea and the larynx on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A part of the human respiratory system has these features: also called the sound box. Identify the part – the trachea or the larynx? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) The trachea: straight tube extending to the mid-thoracic cavity; divides at the fifth thoracic vertebra; supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings. The larynx: cartilaginous box; helps in sound production; also called the sound box. (b) The larynx.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: the larynx; 1 mark: “also called the sound box” is a feature of the larynx.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The respiratory rhythm centre is in the pons.
Reason (R): Nearly 20–25 per cent of CO₂ is transported by RBCs and 70 per cent as bicarbonate.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false: It is in the medulla; the pneumotaxic centre is in the pons. R is a true statement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Conditions at a site in the body are: low pO₂ (40 mm Hg); high pCO₂ (45 mm Hg). Identify the site. Give a reason.
items.answer: The tissues
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the tissues; 1 mark: the features low pO₂ (40 mm Hg); high pCO₂ (45 mm Hg) are characteristic of it.

items.stem: Which term describes the process by which alveolar air is released out when intra-pulmonary pressure is higher than atmospheric pressure?
items.answer: expiration
items.markingKey: (a) Expiration: the process by which alveolar air is released out when intra-pulmonary pressure is higher than atmospheric pressure.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT an animal that respires through the body surface?
items.answer: birds
items.markingKey: (a) Birds is an animal that respires through lungs, not an animal that respires through the body surface.

items.stem: A phase of breathing has these features: intercostal muscles relax; thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease. Identify the phase. Give a reason.
items.answer: Expiration
items.markingKey: 1 mark: expiration; 1 mark: the features intercostal muscles relax; thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease are characteristic of it.

items.answer: tidal volume – respiratory volume; total lung capacity – pulmonary capacity; inspiratory capacity – pulmonary capacity; residual volume – respiratory volume.
